abstract: The Yale Budget Lab analyzes whether AI adoption has produced detectable effects on the US labor market through early 2026, finding no statistically significant impact on aggregate employment or wages despite rapid AI adoption across industries. The analysis examines standard labor market indicators — payroll employment, unemployment rates, wage growth, and labor force participation — and finds continued labor market strength: unemployment remains low, payrolls are steady, and wage growth has been broadly consistent with pre-AI trends. The authors advance two non-exclusive explanations for the absence of detectable effects. First, AI may simply be too early in its adoption cycle to produce macro-level disruption — historical technology transitions have typically taken 10-20 years to reshape labor markets. Second, current measurement tools may be too coarse to detect the shifts that are actually occurring: AI may be restructuring work within occupations (changing task composition, altering productivity, shifting skill requirements) rather than eliminating occupations outright, and standard labor market surveys are not designed to capture within-occupation task reallocation. The paper cautions against interpreting the absence of evidence as evidence of absence — the lack of macro effects is consistent with both 'AI is overhyped' and 'AI effects are real but not yet measurable' hypotheses.
keyFindings: No statistically significant AI effect on aggregate US employment or wages through early 2026 despite rapid adoption
Labor market indicators remain strong: low unemployment, steady payrolls, consistent wage growth

Absence of detectable effects is consistent with both 'AI is overhyped' and 'effects are real but unmeasurable' hypotheses
methodology: Analysis of standard BLS labor market indicators (CES payroll employment, CPS unemployment, wage series) through early 2026. Examines whether trend breaks coincide with AI adoption acceleration. Yale Budget Lab research note. Specific econometric methods not available from truncated web content.
